newsitem.title: SPAIN: Endesa case raises doubts before sale.
newsitem.headline: Endesa case raises doubts before sale.

text.p: The Spanish stock market commission's decision to file suit against Endesa has prompted new uncertainty over the electricity group at a key time ahead of the state's planned sale of its 66 percent stake.
Despite having damaged the credibility of the firm's management and by implication that of the government, the move should only have a limited impact on the shares, analysts said.

Stock market commission CNMV said late on Wednesday that it would start proceedings against Empresa Nacional de Electricidad (Endesa), its chairman and its finance director for a "very serious infraction" of bourse regulations.
Endesa had failed to tell the authority about its plans to bid for 75 percent of regional utilities Fuerzas Electricas de Catalunya (Fecsa) and Sevillana de Electricidad in October, the CNMV said.

Endesa issued a statement on Thursday denying the charges, adding that it trusted the case would "conclude finally with the total exoneration of responsibility by the firm and its management". The Industry Ministry declined to comment.

On October 10 a local financial newspaper had published news of the possible takeover. But when the CNMV subsequently made a routine enquiry into the report, Endesa denied that it was to launch a bid for shares in the two companies.
Then on October 18, Endesa made the bid official.
By not telling the CNMV the electricity firm now risks being heavily fined. The amount can be up to a fifth of shareholders' equity, according to bourse regulations.

The news comes at a sensitive time, with the government planning to start the sale of its remaining 66 percent stake in the key utility in mid-1997. The placement is planned to go ahead in three tranches.

Shares in Endesa moved lower on Thursday as analysts assessed the impact of the news. By early afternoon, the stock had shed 60 pesetas, or 0.68 percent, to 8,750, while the Ibex-35 index of leading shares moved up 0.71 percent to 4,849.72.
Analysts agreed that the case should not delay the privatisation timetable. The most serious consequence would be that chairman Feliciano Fuster could step down but that was not viewed too gravely.
"I think the only effect it's going to have is to provide an invitation for Fuster to leave...but we were expecting that before the placement anyway," said an analyst at a European bank.

It has been thought likely that Fuster would step down since the new conservative government took over from the Socialists earlier this year. There have been significant changes on the boards of most partially state-owned firms since then.
One dealer said the affair was most damaging in terms of the credibility of both Endesa and the government.
"It's pretty shoddy really. It doesn't look good from abroad, although the consequences should be limited" he said.
